**Abstract**

**Background:** Heteroclitic peptides, generated by single amino acid substitutions in wild-type epitopes, represent a promising strategy to enhance T cell receptor (TCR) recognition and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) binding. However, the impact of substitutions in TCR-facing positions on MHC-I binding remains incompletely characterized. In this study, we identified and characterized heteroclitic variants of two well-characterized epitopes, the melanoma-associated Trp2 and the HPV-derived E7, focusing on modifications at TCR-binding positions and their effects on H-2Db binding.

**Methods:** A complete panel of 171 (9 × 19) single-position variants was generated for each wild-type epitope by sequentially replacing every residue with all 20 amino acids. Binding to the H-2Db MHC-I molecule was predicted using the NetMHCpan 4.0 algorithm. Variants showing improved binding and harboring substitutions in the TCR-facing position 4 (p4) were selected for further in silico and structural analysis. Three-dimensional models of the peptide–H-2Db complexes were built by homology modeling using the crystallographic structure of H-2Db in complex with the KAVYNFATC peptide (PDB entry 1F2) as a template, and the resulting complexes were analyzed by molecular docking.

**Results:** Most substitutions reduced H-2Db binding relative to the wild-type sequence; however, 47 Trp2 and 45 E7 heteroclitic variants were predicted to bind with higher affinity than their respective wild-type epitopes. Notably, modifications at the TCR-facing p4 residue, which does not directly contact H-2Db, substantially influenced peptide binding. For the weak-binder Trp2 (wild-type affinity: 6990 nM), p4 substitutions increased H-2Db binding up to 9.5-fold (best variant: 735 nM). In the E7 epitope, replacement of the polar Tyrosine at p4 broadly improved binding regardless of the chemical properties of the substituting residue, with the non-polar Valine and the polar Glutamine yielding the greatest gains; the non-polar Tryptophan was the sole exception. A similar pattern was observed for Trp2, where the polar Glutamine substituting the negatively charged Aspartic Acid produced the most pronounced improvement. Structural modeling revealed that the E7 epitope shares an Asn residue at position 5 (N5) with the template peptide, serving as a key anchor for H-2Db interaction, whereas the Trp2 epitope lacked an equivalent anchoring residue, providing a structural rationale for its weak binding.

**Conclusions:** Substitutions at TCR-facing positions, particularly p4, can markedly improve MHC-I binding of otherwise weak epitopes without directly engaging the MHC groove. These findings identify heteroclitic peptides with enhanced H-2Db-binding efficacy and provide a structural basis for designing optimized peptide ligands for immunotherapy.
